crm_note.headline: Lukas Brandt: Brackenvane first round (coding) done; he called it mixed; awaiting feedback
crm_note.how_it_went: Lukas described the round as mixed. He said the first half (lock-free ring buffer, memory ordering, false sharing) was really good. He was not sure about the second half (order book), where he ran out of time with a bug in the cancel path, and said he was annoyed with himself.

rounds.format: Part of a 90-minute coding round with Raj and Ellie, two engineers from the execution tech team. Shared editor, C++20, no compiler at first.
asked: Write a lock-free single-producer single-consumer ring buffer
Memory ordering for head and tail, including Ellie asking why not use seq_cst everywhere
What happens if head and tail sit on the same cache line (false sharing)
rounds.candidate_view: Said the first half was really good. He used atomics for head and tail with a power-of-two size, release on the tail store, acquire on the other side and relaxed for a thread reading its own index. He explained the fence cost of seq_cst on the hot path. On false sharing he covered padding to 64 bytes, alignas and padding more on some chips because of the adjacent line prefetcher. He thinks they liked it. Raj wrote something down and Lukas was unsure whether that was good or bad.

rounds.format: Same session, with a compiler turned on
asked: Build an order book with price levels and add, modify and cancel, with fast best bid and ask
Raj asked what std::map does to the cache
rounds.candidate_view: Not sure about this half. He started with std::map, then talked about a flat array indexed by price tick with a bitmap to find the best level. He ran out of time before it worked: it compiled but the cancel path had a bug. Ellie told him they don't expect people to finish and want to see how candidates move off the naive version. He said he is annoyed with himself.

asked: How to measure latency and know a change made things faster
Whether he has used kernel bypass
Virtual functions versus templates on the hot path
rounds.candidate_view: Gave answers: rdtsc, pinned cores, warm versus cold cache, looking at the tail (99.9th percentile) not the mean. He has used kernel bypass on the market data side. He suggested CRTP and explained why. He gave no view on how these went.

compensation.expectation: £145k, unchanged from what he told Tom before
compensation.notes: Tom said this fits Brackenvane's band.

crm_note.notice_and_non_compete: Eight weeks' notice. No non-compete: Quarnby is a vendor and does not use them.
competing_processes: One other trading firm, first round in the week starting 2026-11-16
risks: Worried about hours at a prop firm because he has a young child at home. Tom said this is better asked at the next round with the head of team, and said he will find out what he can.
Another trading firm has a first round in the week starting 2026-11-16, so that process could run in parallel.

next_actions.action: Find out what he can about working hours in the team
Let Lukas know as soon as feedback comes in
next_actions.due: as soon as Tom hears (said on the call)

next_actions.action: Brackenvane to come back on the first round. The interviewers said they move fast. If he progresses, the next round would be a system design round (market data handler end to end) and a chat with the head of the team.
next_actions.due: a week maybe (said on the call)

candidate.subject: Brackenvane Trading first round: next steps
candidate.body:
Hi Lukas,

Thanks for talking me through the first round at Brackenvane Trading today.

Raj and Ellie told you they move fast, possibly within a week. They said the next stage would be a system design round, designing a market data handler end to end, followed by a chat with the head of the team.

On the hours question, it is a fair thing to ask, and the head of team round is a better place to raise it than me guessing. In the meantime I will find out what I can.

Your details are as we discussed: eight weeks' notice, no non-compete, and £145k, which fits their band.

I will let you know as soon as I hear from Brackenvane.

Best wishes,
Tom

client.subject: Lukas Brandt: first round feedback
client.body:
Hi,

Thank you for interviewing Lukas Brandt for the Low-Latency C++ Developer role.

When you have had a chance to gather the interviewers' views, I would be grateful for your feedback. I would also be glad to hear your thoughts on next steps.

Best wishes,
Tom

process.format: 90 minutes in a shared editor using C++20. In the first half there is no compiler; they want to watch you write code. The second half has a compiler switched on and an order book task.
process.who: Two engineers from the execution tech team, Raj and Ellie
process.what_they_look_for: Lock-free and cache-aware design, a clear grasp of memory ordering, and how you measure latency. On the order book, Ellie said they do not expect people to finish. They want to see how you would move off the naive version.

process.format: Design a market data handler end to end

process.round: Chat with the head of the team

question_themes.theme: Lock-free data structures and memory ordering
examples: Write a lock-free single-producer single-consumer ring buffer
Questions on memory ordering for the head and tail indices
Why not just use seq_cst everywhere?
What happens if head and tail sit on the same cache line?
Build an order book with price levels, add, modify and cancel, with fast access to the best bid and ask
What does that do to your cache? (asked about a std::map version)
How would you know your change made things faster?

question_themes.theme: Hot path design and low-latency experience
examples: Virtual functions versus templates on the hot path
Whether you have used kernel bypass

tripped_people_up: Starting the order book with std::map drew an immediate question from Raj: "what does that do to your cache".
advice: Be ready to explain the memory ordering for a lock-free SPSC ring buffer, store by store and load by load. Be ready to say why you would not use seq_cst everywhere on the hot path.
Practise writing C++20 without a compiler, since the first half of the coding round has none.

On the order book, expect to be pushed off a std::map version straight away. Have a cache-friendly design ready to describe and build early, because the interviewers want to see how you move off the naive version.
Have a clear method for showing that a change made code faster, covering how you set up the measurement and which statistics you look at.
Know the trade-offs between virtual functions and templates on the hot path, and be able to explain your choice.
For the system design round, prepare to design a market data handler end to end.
logistics: The first round lasts 90 minutes in a shared editor using C++20. There is no compiler at first, and a compiler is switched on for the second half.
After the first round there is a system design round, then a chat with the head of the team. The firm said it moves fast, a week maybe.
For a different role at the firm, an interviewer asked about notice period and non-compete in the second round.
Your notice period is eight weeks and you have no non-compete.
